children: By Ella Cao and Lewis Jackson

China's soybean imports fell in August from a year earlier, but rose from July and increased over the eight months to August, customs data showed on Tuesday, supported by Brazil's bumper soybean crop, smooth port logistics and steady domestic feed demand.
The world's largest soybean buyer brought in 12.14 million metric tons in August, down 1.1% from 12.28 million tons a year earlier and up 5.7% from July.
Imports totalled 74.11 million tons in the January to August period, up 1.1% from 73.33 million tons a year earlier, the data showed.

"The month-on-month rise in imports and the increase in January to August volumes were partly driven by Brazil's bumper 2025/26 soybean harvest and smooth port logistics," said Liu Jinlu, an agricultural researcher at Guoyuan Futures.
"Domestic livestock and poultry herds also remained at a certain scale, supporting underlying crushing demand for soybean meal."
FULL-YEAR IMPORTS SEEN FLAT OR SLIGHTLY LOWER THAN 2025
Three analysts expect China's full-year soybean imports to be broadly unchanged or slightly lower than last year's record 111.83 million tons.
"A gradual decline in China's breeding sow herd is likely to cap pig feed demand growth in the fourth quarter, weighing on soybean demand," Liu said.

Rosa Wang, an analyst at Shanghai JC Intelligence Co., said soybean arrivals were expected to total about 35 million metric tons from August through November, with fourth-quarter arrivals declining month by month in line with seasonal patterns.

Chinese private crushers are facing high import costs and weak margins ahead of President Xi Jinping's expected visit to the U.S. later this month, with traders hoping for tariff relief that would widen their sourcing options as South American supplies near the end of their marketing season.

State-owned buyers are estimated to have bought more than 11 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans after a meeting between the two countries' leaders in May left an existing commitment to purchase 25 million tons annually through 2028 unchanged.
